6.127.m: Kārtavīrya said: / 'For what reason, O brahmin sage, is the exceedingly wonderful power / in the Māgha bath described? Tell me that, O you of noble vows!
Since that merchant was freed from sin by one [bath] and went to heaven by a second / through the merit of Māgha, tell me that curiosity.'
it removes impurity, O tiger among men, it dissolves, destroys heat, / saves all beings, and provides nourishment and life.
The waters are the god Nārāyaṇa—so it is recited in all the Vedas. / Just as the sun is supreme among planets, and the moon among asterisms, / so Māgha is the best of months in all rites.
When the sun is in Capricorn in Māgha, in the early morning and in clear weather, / a bath even in water the size of a cow's footprint grants heaven even to sinners.
This conjunction, O king, is hard to attain in the three worlds, moving and unmoving; / in this conjunction, even an incapable person, if he should bathe for three days,
or should give something, even if incapable, desiring the non-existence of poverty— / even by three baths in Māgha, men become wealthy and long-lived.
For five or seven days the fruit increases like the moon. / When the sun in Capricorn has arrived, which is holy and bestows merit upon mortals,
all lunar days are to be honored in acts such as bathing and giving; / they cause the performer here to attain the imperishable, eternal abode.
Therefore one should bathe outdoors in Māgha, desiring one's own welfare. / Now I will explain the supreme rule for the Māgha bath.
Some observance in the form of a vow must be undertaken by the best of men; / for the sake of an extraordinary fruit, the wise man should abandon some food.
One should sleep on the ground; ghee mixed with sesame seeds is to be offered in the fire; / and one should worship eternal Viṣṇu Vāsudeva at the three divisions of the day.
An unbroken lamp should be given, dedicated to the god Mādhava; / [and one should give] firewood, blankets, clothing, sandals, saffron, and ghee.'
Oil, a cotton storage vessel, raw cotton, a quilted cotton jacket, a woven cloth, / and food should be given according to one's means in Māgha, O king.
Likewise, one should give gold, even a single raktikā in weight, to a knower of the Veda; / that gift is inexhaustible, O king, always just like [the merits gained at] the ocean.
One should not warm oneself at another's fire, and one should abstain from receiving gifts; / at the end of Māgha, one should feed brāhmaṇas according to one's means, O ruler of men.
And a sacrificial fee should be given to them by one desiring one's own welfare; / likewise, the concluding rite of Māgha [should be performed] according to the rules of Ekādaśī.
It should be performed with faith by one desiring imperishable heaven, / for the sake of attaining endless merit, and in order to please Viṣṇu.
“While the sun is in Capricorn in the month of Māgha, O Govinda, O Acyuta, O Mādhava! / By this bath, O Lord, become the bestower of the fruit described.”
Uttering this mantra, one should bathe, silent and collected, / and remember again Vāsudeva, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Mādhava.
Even at home, a water jar touched by the wind at night— / a bath from that is like [a bath at] a sacred ford, yielding the fruit of all desires.
There, by one under a vow, [the jar] should be given with food and accompanied by utensils; / through the power of that bath, a man will not go to hell.
The bath with warm water that is taken by men at home / yields the fruit of six years indeed when the sun is in Capricorn.
An outdoor bath in a step-well and the like is considered to yield the fruit of twelve years; / in a reservoir, O king, it is twice as much, and in a river fourfold.
It is a hundredfold in holy basins of the gods, and a hundredfold in a great river; / it is four hundredfold, O king, at the confluence of great rivers.
All that fruit is multiplied a thousandfold when the sun is in Capricorn / by the mere bath in the Gaṅgā, O king, which a man obtains.

Those who plunge into the Gaṅgā in the month of Māgha, O best of kings, / do not fall from the abode of the gods for a thousand sets of four ages.

A thousand gold coins every day, O ruler of men, / is given by him into the Gaṅgā who bathes in the month of Māgha.
A thousand multiplied by a hundred, O best of kings, in Māgha / is declared by the sages [as the fruit of] bathing at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
For burning away the heavy burden of the multitude of sins, Prajāpati / established Prayāga, O king, intent on the welfare of creatures.
Hear properly of this place of white and black waters indeed, / established long ago by Brahmā for the sacrificial beasts that are sins.
Even if accompanied by a hundred sins, one who plunges into the white and black waters / in Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn never sinks into wombs.
Even a mortal engaged in slaughter who takes a bath at Prayāga / in the month of Māgha, O tiger among men, goes to the supreme abode.
The white and black current filled internally with the Sarasvatī— / that very path to the world of Viṣṇu did the Creator fashion.
Difficult to cross is the Vaiṣṇava illusion, hard even for the gods to conquer; / but at Prayāga, it is burnt away in the month of Māgha, O ruler of men.
Having enjoyed pleasures in radiant worlds manifold times, / they later merge into the bearer of the discus, through the Māgha immersion at Prayāga.
When one bathes at the white and black [confluence] in Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn, / even Citragupta is not able to count that merit.
When one immerses in the white and black [confluence] in Māgha with [the sun] in Capricorn, / even Brahmā is incapable of describing the glorification of that merit.
The fruit of fasting without food for a full hundred years— / that is the fruit of a three-day bath at Prayāga in the month of Māgha.
What fruit [is gained] by a thousand bhāras of gold at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse, / one obtains day after day in Māgha from bathing at the Veṇī.
The unimpaired fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices, O king, / surely belongs to baths in the white and black [waters] in Māgha.
Whatever sacred places and the seven holy cities exist on earth, / they come to the Veṇī to bathe in the month of Māgha, O best of kings.
All the sacred places, blackened by the fault of contact with sinners, / become white-colored from the Māgha immersion at Prayāga.
The sin accumulated over an eon through births by men, O king, / is reduced to ashes for those who have bathed in Māgha in the white and black [waters].

The sin born of speech, mind, and body of a man dissolves, / certainly, for one who has bathed for three days at Prayāga in the month of Māgha.

A person who bathes for three days at Prayāga in the month of Māgha / sheds sin and goes to heaven, as a serpent sheds its old skin.
The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever one plunges into it; / ten times more meritorious than that is where it meets the Vindhya.
A hundred times more than that is the Gaṅgā flowing northwards at Kāśī; / a hundred times more than Kāśī is it declared to be at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
A thousand times greater than those is it when flowing to the west, / which, O king, by its mere sight destroys [the sin of] brāhmaṇa-slaughter.
The west-flowing Gaṅgā united with the Kālindī / destroys sins committed in ten million [lives]; it is hard to attain in Māgha, O king.
What is spoken of as nectar, O king, that is famed as the Veṇī on earth; / a muhūrta in it in Māgha is hard to attain even for the gods.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, the Rudras, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts, / Gandharvas, world guardians, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Pannagas,
Siddhas endowed with powers such as atomicity, and others who teach the ultimate truth, / Brahmāṇī, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Śacī, Menā, Aditi, and Diti,
all those wives of the gods, and likewise the serpent women, O king, / Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā,
all the hosts of Apsarases, and likewise the hosts of ancestors— / they all come to bathe in Māgha at the Veṇī, O ruler of men.
In their own forms in the Kṛta age, and in disguised forms in the Kali age, / [they come;] the fruit of a three-day bath at Prayāga in the month of Māgha,
one cannot obtain on earth even through a thousand horse sacrifices. / In ancient times Kāñcanamālinī gave the fruit of a three-day bath in Māgha

to a rākṣasa, O king, by which that evildoer was liberated.
Kārtavīrya said: / O Blessed One, who was that rākṣasa, and who was Kāñcanamālinī?

How did she bestow religious merit, or how did he attain the good path? / Tell this, O lord of yogins, sun of the lineage of Atri! / If you deem it should be heard, great indeed is my curiosity.
Dattātreya said:
Hear, O king, a wonderful ancient legendary history, / by the mere remembrance of which one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
There was an Apsaras endowed with beauty named Kāñcanamālinī; / having bathed at Prayāga in the month of Māgha, she was going to the abode of Śiva.
By an old rakṣas standing in a bower of the king of mountains, / having the form of a mountain, she was seen ascending into the sky.
Radiant, of fine golden hue, with beautiful hips and long eyes, / moon-faced, with lovely hair, and full, elevated breasts—
seeing her endowed with beauty, the rākṣasa then said: / “Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? Whence do you come?
Why is your garment wet, and whence is your braid of hair moist? / Where are you going, O timid one, and whence is your sky-faring gait?
Or by what merit, O auspicious lady, has your radiant body, / exceedingly endowed with beauty and charming, come to be?
By the falling of a drop [of water] from your garment upon my head, O fair-eyed one, / my mind, which was always cruel, instantly found peace.
What greatness belongs to this water? Please explain this. / You seem virtuous to me; such a form cannot be devoid of virtues.”

My upper garment is wet, for I bathed well in the Sitāsita [waters];
now, O rākṣasa, I must go to Kailāsa, the best of mountains.

There abides the lord of Pārvatī, worshipped by gods and asuras.
By the power of the water from the confluence, your cruelty, O rākṣasa, has vanished.

I shall tell you all about the religious merit by which
I was born as a celestial maiden, the daughter of the wise gandharva.

I was once a courtesan of the king, the lord of Kaliṅga,
endowed with beauty and grace, proud of my good fortune and youth.

In that city, I was the crest-jewel of all the other young women.
In that lifetime, O rākṣasa, having enjoyed pleasures at will,

the entire city was enchanted by me through my abundance of youth.
Various jewels, ornaments, wealth,

garments of manifold hues, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood—
all this was accumulated by me whose form was bewitching.

I knew no end to gold in my dwelling, O night-wanderer!
Afflicted with passion, young men waited upon my feet.

They were all cheated by me of their entire property through deceit;
and through rivalry with one another, some passionate men even died.

In this way my path ran through that whole delightful city.
When old age arrived, my heart began to grieve:
No gifts did I bestow, no oblations did I offer, no mantras did I recite, and no vows did I observe.

I did not gratify the brāhmaṇas, nor did I do what was good for living beings;
not even an atom of merit was done by me out of negligence.

Only sin was committed, O noble one, and because of that my mind burns.
Lamenting thus in many ways, I took refuge in a brāhmaṇa,

a devotee of brāhmaṇas, learned in the Vedas, the priest of that king.
Indeed, O rākṣasa, I asked him: 'How can there be expiation for me?

How, O best of the twice-born, shall I attain a good destiny away from this sin?
Burnt by my own actions, I am wretched and despondent in mind.

Submerged in the mire of sin, lift me up by grasping my hair!
Rain down the water of compassion upon me, O twice-born, with a gaze of joy!

Among good people, all are virtuous; a virtuous one is he who is virtuous toward the unvirtuous.'
Having heard this speech of mine, he showed mercy toward me.

The twice-born said:
'I know of all your forbidden conduct, O fair-faced one.
Quickly follow my word: go to the sacred field of Prajāpati.

Having gone there, bathe; by that your sin will be destroyed.
All that was in your mind, O blessed one, has been grieved over by me.

I see no other way for the destruction of your sin;
the sages have declared bathing in a sacred ford to be the supreme expiation.

However, O timid one, one should abandon at the sacred ford whatever evil was done even in thought.
Purified by the bath at Prayāga, you will surely go to heaven.

By mere bathing at Prayāga, there is heaven for men, without doubt.
Sin committed in any other place, O beautiful woman,

perishes at Prayāga, except for sin committed at a sacred ford.
Listen, O timid one! In former times, Śakra, seeing the wife of the sage Gautama,

fell under the sway of desire and went to her as a secret lover.
By that terrible sin, the fruit was brought forth immediately.

For Indra, violator of a sage’s wife, before her very eyes,
his body became vile, despised, and shameful in this manner,

marked with a thousand vulvas by the power of her husband's curse.
With downcast face, the king of the gods departed from there.

He blamed his own deed, overcome [with remorse] and ashamed.
On the summit of Meru, abundant in water and a hundred yojanas wide,

having gone there, he entered the bud of a golden lotus.
Staying there, he constantly reviled himself and the god of love:

'Fie on that lustful nature in this world, which instantly yields sin,
by which, despised by all the world, one surely goes to hell!

It destroys lifespan, fame, renown, dharma, and fortitude.
Fie on the ill-behaved god of love, the certain abode of misfortunes,

dwelling in the body, hard to subdue, rejoicing an enemy, and always unruly!'
While Indra, concealed in the lotus-dwelling, was speaking thus,

the world of the gods did not shine without Indra, O timid one.
Then the gods along with the gandharvas, the world-protectors, and the kinnaras,

accompanied by Śacī, approached Bṛhaspati and asked:
'O holy one, we do not know where Lord Indra is.

Where is he staying? Where has he gone? Or where should we search for him?
Without him, heaven does not shine along with the hosts of gods,

just as a family endowed with fortune and virtue does not shine without a good son.
Let a means be devised quickly, so that the celestial realm may shine

as having a protector and blessed with beauty; no delay is proper here.'
Having heard their words, the guru spoke these words:

'I know where he stays out of shame for his own transgression;
Maghavan is reaping the fruit of an act done out of rashness.

Terrible are the consequences for mortals from the abandonment of righteous conduct.
Alas, intoxicated with pride of sovereignty, not reflecting on what ought and ought not to be done,

he performed a blameworthy act that destroys both the seen and unseen [fruits],
just as fools do when their minds are struck down by fate,

so that because of transgression, life here and hereafter becomes fruitless.
Now let us go there, where Śakra stays.'
Having spoken thus, all of them went out, with Bṛhaspati at their head, / seeing a grove of golden lotuses in the wide lake.

they praised the king of the gods, so that he would be awakened.
Then, awakened by his guru, he came forth from the lotus bud,

wretched-faced, deformed, with eyes narrowed from shame;
Indra grasped the feet of his guru, the twice-born.

'Save me! Tell me the expiation for this sin, O Bṛhaspati!'
Having heard the speech of the king of gods, the brāhmaṇa Bṛhaspati said:

'Listen, O lord of the gods, I shall declare the means to destroy sin:
By mere bathing at Prayāga, at that very moment

you will be freed from sin, O king of the gods; let us go there together with you.'
Then, arriving along with the priest, the slayer of Bala

bathed in the Sitāsita ford and was immediately freed from sins.
Then the guru of the gods, pleased, granted him a boon:

'By the mere bath at Prayāga, your sin has been wiped away, O sinless one.
For you whose sin has ended, O Śakra, by my grace, quickly

this thousand of vulvas shall become a thousand eyes for you!'
Right then, by the word of the twice-born, the lord of Śacī shone

with a thousand eyes, like Lake Mānasa with lotuses.
Then, worshipped by all the gods and sages,

and praised by the gandharvas, Śakra went to Amarāvatī.
In this way, Indra was instantly freed from sin at Prayāga.

You too must go, O auspicious lady, to Prayāga, resort of the gods,
for the instant destruction of sin and for an assured journey to heaven.'
Having heard his words along with the auspicious legendary history, / being instantly filled with awe, bowing at the feet of the twice-born,

abandoning all my kinsmen, male and female servants, and home,
and completely leaving all objects of sense like mouthfuls of poison, O rākṣasa,
Seeing my body to be destroyed in an instant, I departed, / burning then with an inner fire, terrible with falling into the ocean of hell,
in my heart, O tiger among corpses! Agonized by that, / I went and bathed in the month of Māgha at the black-and-white [confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā].
Hear the glorious power of that bath, O aged night-stalker: / in three days my sin was destroyed; with twenty-seven days,
by the remaining merit that came to me, I attained divine status, / delighting on Mount Kailāsa as a beloved companion of the Mountain's Daughter.
I also became one who remembers past lives through the power of Prayāga. / Remembering the glory of Prayāga, I go there every month of Māgha.
"Thus, O rākṣasa, whatever was asked by you with an astonished mind, / all that narrative has been related by me for your satisfaction."
For my pleasure, do you tell me your own story, O rākṣasa! / By what action were you born deformed, exceedingly terrible,

bearded, long-fanged, and a flesh-eater in a mountain cave?
The rākṣasa said: / A good person gives what is desired, receives, speaks a secret, and inquires,
with affection, O auspicious lady; and all that is present in you. / Honored by you, indeed, O fair-eyed one, I think
an immediate expiation is about to happen through you for this person of cruel deeds. / Therefore I shall tell you, O blessed lady, the wrongdoing that I myself committed.
Having disclosed his sorrow to a good person, anyone would become happy thereafter. / Hear, O woman of beautiful hips! In Kāśī I was a Ṛgvedic scholar, master of the Veda,
born formerly as a foremost twice-born in a great, stainless family. / From wicked kings, O timid lady, and likewise from Śūdras and Vaiśyas,
a dreadful, corrupt acceptance of gifts was made by me in Vārāṇasī, / repeatedly, manifold times, forbidden and highly contemptible.
Corrupt gifts even from an outcaste were not refused by me. / And another transgression occurred there for me of foolish mind; / there was no wicked deed that was not committed there by me.

And hear another fault concerning the sacred site, O woman of fine complexion! / Whatever sin is an atom's measure in Avimukta turns into Mount Meru; / yet no dharma whatsoever had been accumulated by me in that birth.
Then after a long time I died right there, O beautiful lady; / but through the power of Avimukta I did not go to hell.
Anyone who dies in Avimukta, even if sinful, does not go to hell; / yet any sin committed in Avimukta becomes firm like an adamantine bolt.
By that sin coated like an adamantine plaster, my birth as a rākṣasa arose— / a terrible, exceedingly cruel sin produced on the snow mountain.
I was born twice previously in the womb of a vulture, thrice as a tiger, twice as a snake; / once as an owl, and after that as a village pig.
Now this tenth birth of mine, O passionate lady, is that of a rākṣasa. / A thousand years have passed for me in this birth.
There is no expiation for me, O blessed lady, from this ocean of sorrow. / For three leagues around here, O fair-browed one, it was made devoid of creatures by me,
and the destruction of many innocent beings was committed. / By that deed, O fair-browed one, my mind is constantly burned.
Sprinkled with the nectar of seeing you, my mind has attained coolness. / A holy bathing-place bears fruit in time, but the company of the virtuous does so immediately.
Therefore, O fair-browed one, the wise praise the company of the virtuous. / This entire sorrow residing in my heart has been told to you by me.
A good person whose own heart is not distressed is rare, O fair-browed one. / For you know what is fitting here; I will say nothing beyond this.
Reflecting on how I might reach the other shore of this ocean of sorrow: / the prosperity of good people is a livelihood for all.

Does the Ocean of Milk give its milk only to the swan and not to the crane?
Dattātreya said: / Having heard his speech, her mind moistened with compassion,
making up her mind to give merit, Kāñcanamālinī sang: / "I shall make an expiation, O rākṣasa; now truly do not grieve!
Having made a firm vow, I will strive for your liberation. / Indeed, many Māgha [vows] were observed year after year according to rule
with faith by me, O good one, in the sacred field of Brahmā at the black-and-white [confluence]. / I shall tell you the account of the merit of that, O rākṣasa.
Merit should indeed be kept secret, so have wise people said; / the sages who expound the Veda praise giving to the afflicted.
O good one, what fruit would there be for a cloud that rains upon the ocean? / The fruit born of that merit was experienced by myself, O rākṣasa;
I will give that to you, O friend, which instantly destroys sin." / Then, having wrung out her garment and taken water in her lotus hands,
she gave the merit born of Māgha to that aged rākṣasa. / Hear, O king, the wondrous power born of the religious merit of Māgha!
Instantly upon receiving that merit, his rākṣasa body was cast off; / he assumed the form of a deity, his appearance radiant like the sun,
mounted upon a celestial chariot, his eyes wide open with joy, / shining then in the sky, illuminating the directions with his splendor.
Assuming a divine form, he shone like a second sun. / Then he praised that Kāñcanamālinī:
“O blessed lady, the divine Lord who bestows the fruit of actions knows / that all this benefit has been done by you in a state where there was no expiation for me.
Even now, out of compassion be pleased and grant your favor; / give me instruction, O goddess, which consists of all good conduct and is auspicious,
which surely produces all virtue, so that I commit no sin! / Having heard that and received your permission, I shall go afterwards to the abode of the gods.”
Dattātreya said: / Hearing this beloved speech consisting of righteousness uttered by him, / Kāñcanamālinī declared righteousness with great affection, O king:

“Practice righteousness constantly, abandon injury to creatures, serve virtuous men, slay the enemy that is desire! / Quickly giving up the proclamation of another's faults and virtues, speak the truth, worship Hari, and go to the world of the gods!

Abandon your notion of self in the body of bone, flesh, and blood; forever release possessiveness regarding wife, sons, and the like! / Unceasingly see this world as transient in a moment; be one who delights in the sentiment of detachment and devoted to yoga!

The path of dharma has been proclaimed by me to you with affection; keep it all in your mind, and be endowed with good conduct! / Having abandoned the body of a rākṣasa, having assumed a divine body, luminous, go quickly to heaven as you please!”
Having heard dharma, delighted and contented, the rākṣasa said: / “May you be always joyful! May there always be auspiciousness for you!
As long as the moon and sun endure, may you delight on Kailāsa in the presence of Śiva! / May there be unbroken love for you from Umā, O woman of fine complexion!
Be devoted to dharma, devoted to austerities always, O mother! / Let there be no greed in you for the body; always remove the distress of the afflicted!”
Having spoken thus and bowed to that virtuous Kāñcanamālinī, / the rākṣasa went to heaven, praised by many gandharvas.
Divine maidens, having arrived then, showered rains of flowers / upon the head of that Kāñcanamālinī, filled with joy.
Having embraced her, the maidens then spoke pleasant words: / “A wondrous release of the rākṣasa has been accomplished by you, O blessed lady!
Out of fear of this wicked one, no one would enter this forest; / now, free from fear, we wander here as we please.”
Hearing that speech of theirs, O king, Kāñcanamālinī, / joyful by that very gift, was then a virtuous woman who had accomplished her purpose.
Having quickly released that rākṣasa, the excellent Gandharva maiden Kāñcanamālinī, / playing with them, departed for Hara's abode, filled with delight and the desire to do good to others.

6.127.m:
And whatever man should hear with supreme devotion this dialogue spoken by that excellent girl, / is never at any time afflicted by rākṣasas, and his mind turns deeply to righteousness.

Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, / in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the glorification of the month of Māgha, in the dialogue between Dilīpa and Vasiṣṭha, [ends the chapter] named "The Liberation of the Rākṣasa."

"The glorification of Māgha as spoken by Dattātreya has been told. / Now I shall explain the fruit of bathing in Māgha.

Bathing in Māgha is the best of all sacrifices, granting the fruit of every gift, / equal to all vows and austerities, O scorcher of foes.

Purified in mind through the Māgha bath, placing the ancestors of both families in heaven, / with radiant faces they themselves proceed to heaven in beautiful celestial chariots moving at will.

Those men who, though doing evil at all times, are ever devoted to misconduct and go astray, / if they bathe in Māgha and worship Hari, even they cast off here a multitude of great sins.

Even those men devoid of truth, causing sorrow to father and mother, outside the stages of life, devoid of family duties, / and hypocrites, attain the destination of the virtuous through the baths taken here in Māgha.

A bath in sacred holy places during the month of Māgha is very rare for humans on earth; / because from it the realm of those who know Brahman is attained by men, there is no doubt in my mind about this.

Austerity, charity, muttering prayers, residing in a sacred place, and worshipping Hari during Māgha bring imperishable reward, O king; / therefore, bathing with effort according to one's ability, clothing, food, and gold should be given by men.

The giver of food in Māgha drinks nectar in the abode of the gods; the giver of gold dwells near Indra; / a man who constantly gives a lamp, fire, and clothes dwells, full of splendor, in the world of the sun.

Sinners do not become so purified here by sacrifices, generous gifts, brilliant penances, / chaste studenthood, worship, and practice of yoga as through the baths originating from the merit of Māgha.

Even evildoers do not go to the torment of Yama, the burning multitude of sorrows and unbearable pain, / who bathe in an excellent sacred ford in the month of Māgha while the solar disc is half-risen.

Those who bathe in Māgha and worship Hari become kings when fallen from heaven— / auspicious, handsome, fortunate, pleasant of speech, endowed with righteousness, possessing abundant wealth, and living a hundred years.

6.127.m:
Just as a heap of wood cast into a blazing fire is instantly reduced to nothing but ashes here, / so through bathing in Māgha even a vast accumulation of sins and great offenses is dissolved.

Whatever sin, known or unknown, committed by men with body, speech, or mind, / a bath in Māgha taken in an excellent holy place burns entirely, like Viṣṇu entering the heart.

When, O king, even the fruit of sin being experienced at any time by humans through negligence / is touched by a bath in Māgha, it is certainly destroyed at once.

O lord of the earth, the Gandharva maidens, experiencing the inescapable fruit of sin born of a curse, / were indeed freed through the bath taken in the month of Māgha, by the wondrous word spoken of old by Lomaśa.

Sūta said: / Having heard this with joy and bowed down to his lotus feet, / the king, humble with supreme faith, asked his family priest:

Tell me, O blessed one: from where did the curse come upon the maidens? / Whose daughters were they? What were their names, and what was their age?

How, through the words of Lomaśa, were they freed from the ripening born of the curse? / Where did they bathe for a month, and how many in number were they?

6.127.m:
Vasiṣṭha said: / Hear, O tiger among kings, the supreme story pregnant with righteousness, / just as a fire-drill is pregnant with fire, producing righteousness as [the drill] produces fire.

There was a Gandharva named Sukhasaṃgīti, whose daughter was Pramodinī; / Suśīlā was the daughter of Suśīla; Susvarā of Svaravedin;

Sutārā of Candrakānta, and Candrikā of Suprabha; / these are the excellent names of those apsarases, O king.

All five were maidens, very equal in age, / radiant like moonlight emerging from the moon.

Moon-faced, having beautiful hair, with lower lips like the sweet nectar of the moon, / delighting the eyes as moonlight delights the night-lotuses,

born as mass of beauty, shapely and charming, / with burgeoning pitcher-like breasts, like lotus plants in spring,

opening their lovely youth like creeper bowers with new shoots, / golden-fair, lustrous like gold, adorned with gold ornaments,

wearing garlands of golden campaka flowers, of golden complexion and fine garments, / [skilled] in smiling scales of musical notes and diverse melodic modulations,

in pastimes of keeping rhythm, in playing the flute and lute, / in the fractions of graceful dance blended with the sound of the mṛdaṅga drum,

and skilled in pastimes such as painting and in the arts— / being such, those maidens revelled in the forest for sport.

Cherished by their fathers, the good maidens wandered in the abode of Kubera; / once out of curiosity the five came together in the month of Mādhava, / maidens gathering mandāra flowers from forest to forest.

To worship Gaurī, those excellent women once went to Lake Acchoda; / having gathered excellent golden lotuses from it along with fine blue lotuses,

and having bathed in the pool bright as beryl, pure crystal, and coral, and donned garments, / in silence they fashioned from sand-grains of gold an image of Umā on an earthen altar.

Worshipping Gaurī, anointed with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, with excellent lotuses and other offerings / and manifold articles, filled with deep devotion, the maidens danced to rhythmic patterns.

Then, having taken the excellent gāndhāra note, those doe-eyed maidens sang / a sweet song with very high-pitched sounds and fine modulations, melodious in its syllables, a charming composition with steps.

6.127.m:
While that sweet sound showered delight and joy, and the girls were wholly absorbed in the act of dancing, / there came to the excellent Acchoda ford to bathe the fire-guarding son of the sage Vedanidhi.

He was boundless in beauty, with a face like an excellent lotus, a youth with eyes long like lotus petals, / broad-chested, fair-armed, exceedingly handsome, dark in complexion, like another Kāma.

He shone as a celibate student with a topknot, equipped with a staff like Manmatha with his bow, / wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment, bearing a good sacred thread, his girdle of muñja grass shining like gold around his waist.

Seeing that brāhmaṇa on the bank of the lake, the young women / rejoiced, overcome with wonder: 'Who is this guest for our eyes?'

Abandoning their dancing and singing, intent on gazing at him, / they were like doe struck with arrows by Kāma as if by a hunter.

Saying, 'Look, look!' the five enraptured maidens, in great agitation, / fell into the delusion that that excellent young brāhmaṇa was the god of love himself.

Again and again worshipping him with eyes that were like lotuses, / those maidens afterwards began to deliberate with one another:

"If he is Kāmadeva, how could he wander without Rati? / Or if he is the two Aśvins, those two surely move as a pair.

Is he a Gandharva, or a Kinnara, or a Siddha assuming any form at will, / or a sage's son, or some foremost among men?

Whoever he may be, he was created by the Creator for our sake, / just as a treasure is obtained by a fortunate man through his past deeds.

So has this most excellent bridegroom been brought to us maidens by Gaurī, / her heart softened by the surge of waves of compassion.

'He was chosen by me and by you, and he was chosen by you and by me'— / as the five maidens were thus speaking, O best of kings,

having heard their words there and completed his midday rites, / he too considered in his heart: 'An obstacle has presented itself.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Giriśa, and other gods, and the ancient Siddhas and sages, / even they, mighty in yoga, were effortlessly bewildered by women—how wondrous!

Struck by the archer who bears the makara banner with the sharp arrows of women's eyes / released from the strong bows of their creeper-like eyebrows, whose deer of a mind does not fall, alas?

Only so long does moral prudence shine; only so long does fear of people hold sway; / only so long does firmness of mind endure strongly; only so long is there regard for one's family;

इंद्रजालंस्फुटंवेत्तिमायांजानातिवापुनः
दृष्टोऽप्यदृष्टरूपोऽभूदित्यूचुश्चपरस्परम्
6.127.m:
only so long is there bold mastery of asceticism; only so long is there self-restraint among men, / until women bewilder people with the arrows of their eyes and intoxicating desires.

Let women bewilder and intoxicate the passionate with their charming, alluring arts; / by what qualities will they bewilder and intoxicate me, who am devoted to guarding dharma?

In the vile, impure body of women, fashioned of flesh, semen, feces, and urine, / let the lustful of utterly bewildered mind imagine beauty and take their delight!

For proximity to women has been declared dreadful by the wise endowed with spotless intellect. / Before these women come near, I shall go home at once."

Before those lovely women could come close to him, / by his Vaiṣṇava power the twice-born disappeared.

When he had thus become invisible through his power of yoga, O king, / seeing that wondrous deed of the wise sage's son,

the maidens with frightened eyes, trembling like female deer, / looked toward the ten directions with agitated eyes and blank expressions.

"He surely knows illusion, or understands magic, / for though seen, his form has become invisible," they said to one another.

6.127.m:
Their hearts were constantly filled with the fire of separation, / just like a lush, dense forest engulfed by a blazing wildfire.

"Set aside your illusory art, O beloved, and show yourself quickly! / It is not right for our mind to suffer like a fly in the first bite of food.

Alas, what misery! Why were you shown by the Creator, and why did he join us? / It is understood: you were fashioned for the sake of our great torment!

Is your heart pitiless? Is your mind not upon us? / Are you a rogue, O beloved? Are you stealing away our mind?

Do you have no trust in us? Are you putting us to the test? / Are you fond of playful arts? Are you skilled in illusion?

Do you know the skillful science of entering into our hearts, / and yet do not know the way to exit? Why is this?”

Are you enraged at us without any fault? / Do you know the pain born of deception felt by others?

Without the sight of you, O lord of our heart, / we surely cannot live now; or else we live solely through hope of seeing you again.

Take us also to the place where you have quickly gone! / The Creator who stole away the sight of you has severed the sprout."

6.127.m:
"By all means grant us your sight! By all means show compassion! / Good people never push matters to an extreme!"

Having thus lamented and waited for a long time, / out of fear of their parents the maidens began their swift journey home.

Bound by the chains of love for him, deeply agitated by separation, / somehow taking hold of courage, they returned to their respective homes.

Having arrived, they all collapsed near the water fountain. / Asked by their mothers: "What is this? Why has so much time passed?"

The maidens said: / "Joyfully engaged in singing and playing together with Kinnara maidens, / we remained by the lake, and thus did not notice the passage of the day.

We are exhausted from the road, O mother; because of that there is a fever in our bodies. / Because of our great stupor, we do not have the heart to speak to anyone.”

Having spoken thus, the young girls rolled there on the jeweled floor; / concealing their appearance, those simple-minded ones spoke with their mothers.

One did not joyfully make her pet peacock dance then; / another, out of curiosity, did not teach speech to that parrot in the cage.

Another would not pet the mongoose, nor cheer up the myna; / another, deeply bewildered, did not play with the cranes at all.

6.127.m:
They engaged in no amusements, nor took delight in the palace; / they did not converse with relatives, nor play upon the vīṇā.

They did not drink the nectar-like sweet juice of the wishing-tree's blossoms, / fragrant with mandāra flowers.

Those maidens were just like female yogis with eyes fixed on the tip of their nose, / with an unbroken succession of imperceptible meditations, their minds fixed on the Supreme Person.

On moonstone gems moist with trickling drops of water, / staying at the window for a moment, they would stay by the water fountain for a moment;

for a moment they would make a bed with lotus leaves from the reservoir, / being fanned by their companions with cool plantain leaves.

Thus regarding the night as equal to an eon, those excellent women, / somehow showing fortitude, were agitated as if burning with fever.

In the morning, seeing the jewel of the sky [the sun] and considering it to be their very life, / having informed their respective mothers, they went to worship Gaurī.

Having bathed according to rule, and having performed the worship of the goddess / with flowers and incense as best they could, they remained there singing.

In the meantime, that twice-born youth also came to bathe / from his father's hermitage to that Acchoda lake.

6.127.m:
Seeing the sun at the end of night, just as lotuses bloom, / the maidens became wide-eyed upon seeing that celibate student.

Those maidens went at once into the presence of that celibate student, / and bound him in a noose of arms from left and right.

"You escaped yesterday, O rogue; today you cannot go! / You have surely been chosen by us; let there be no doubt about this!"

Thus addressed, the Brahmin, held fast in their arm-fetters, said: / "By you auspicious, agreeable, and dear words are spoken."

However, for me who am established in the first stage of life, devoted to the study of the Vedas, / my vow in the guru's household has not even today reached its completion.

In whatever stage of life a person is, that duty is to be preserved by the wise. / Therefore, O maidens, I consider this marriage not to be right conduct."

Having heard his words, they then spoke to him, / their voices full of sweet melodies and yearning, like cuckoos in springtime.

"From dharma comes wealth, from wealth comes desire, and from desire comes the emergence of the fruit of dharma. / In just this way the wise describe what the scriptures have determined.

That desire, through the abundance of dharma, has now presented itself before you. / Therefore let this earthly realm of heaven be enjoyed with various delights!"

Hearing those words of theirs, he spoke with a deep voice: / "Your words are true; yet having completed my vow here,

and having obtained the permission of my teacher, I shall perform all the marriage rites, not otherwise." / Having spoken thus, they said again: "Clearly you are a fool, handsome boy!

Divine medicine, the elixir of Brahman, the attainment of a treasure, excellent arts, noble women, / a mantra, and also the elixir of perfection—when these have arrived through dharma, they should not be rejected by a wise man.

Indeed, if a task comes about through fate as accomplished, one who knows conduct does not ignore it. / Since neglect never yields fruit again, dragging it out is not praised.

Maidens full of deep love, pure in family birth, with hearts moist with affection, sweet-voiced, choosing their own husbands, / beautiful indeed, and in lovely youth—only fortunate men obtain them here, and not others.

Where are we, excellent beauties, and where is this ascetic youth? / Indeed, in arranging what is difficult to accomplish, I consider the Creator to be exceedingly wise!

Therefore, you should accept us now, sir, for your auspicious welfare / by the Gāndharva marriage rite; otherwise there is no life for us!"

Having heard their words, the brāhmaṇa, the best knower of dharma, then spoke: / "O fawn-eyed ones, how can dharma be abandoned by men whose only wealth is dharma?

Dharma, wealth, desire, and liberation: this fourfold set, / when pursued as prescribed, is known to be fruitful, but contrary to that it is fruitless.

Being under a vow, I would not take a wife out of season. / One who does not know the proper time for an action does not attain the fruit of the action.

Since my mind is firmly attached to this deliberation of dharma, / therefore listen, O maidens, I do not desire a svayaṃvara.”

Having thus understood his intention and looking at one another, / releasing hand from hand, Pramodinī then grasped his feet.

Suśīlā and Sasvarā seized his two arms, / and Sutārā embraced him, and Candrikā kissed his face.

Even so, he remained undisturbed, like the fire of universal destruction. / Utterly overcome with rage, the student of the Veda cursed them:

"Since you have clung to me like female piśācas, you shall become female piśācas!" / Being cursed thus quickly by him, they released him and stood before him:

"What is this deed, O wicked one, done by you to innocent people? / Having done an unpleasant thing in response to a pleasant act, fie on your knowledge of dharma!

For a man who commits betrayal against those who love him, who are devoted to him, and who are his friends, / happiness is lost in both worlds—so we have heard.

Therefore, you too, by our curse, quickly become a piśāca!" / Having spoken thus, the maidens ceased, sighing and overcome with hunger.

And then, from their mutual fury at that lake, O king, / those maidens and that student of the Veda all entered the state of piśācas.

The female piśācas and that male piśāca, crying out most dreadfully, / were exhausting that fruition of karma previously acquired.

In its own time, good and evil karma acquired before inevitably bears fruit, / inescapable like one's own shadow, even for the gods, O king.

Their fathers cried out, and their mothers there, and his as well; / and for children there is no vigilance—fate is indeed difficult to overcome.

From then on, those piśācas, exceedingly miserable for the sake of food, / running here and there, lived on the bank of the lake.

Thus, after a long time, Lomaśa, the best of sages, / came to Acchoda on the fourteenth day in the month of Pauṣa to bathe.

Seeing that brāhmaṇa, all the piśācas, afflicted with hunger, / running and wishing to kill him, assembled in a pack.

6.127.m:
Being scorched by the extremely fierce splendour of Lomaśa, / unable to stand before him, they all stayed far away.

Just then the brāhmaṇa Vedanidhi arrived there, / and seeing Lomaśa, O king, prostrating with his eight limbs to the ground,

and spoke true and pleasant words, folding his hands at his head: / 'Only when great fortune arises, O vipra, does the company of the virtuous occur.

Between the man who always bathes in all sacred fords beginning with the Gaṅgā / and the one who keeps company with the good, the company of the good is superior.

Association with preceptors, O brāhmaṇa, yields visible and invisible fruits on earth; / it grants heaven and removes disease, but it is considered difficult of access."

Having spoken thus, he related the wonderful past account: / "These are daughters of a gandharva, and this youth is my son."

All of them, in the form of piśācas, deluded by their mutual curse, / stand with miserable faces before you, O best of sages.

By your sight, the deliverance of the youths will take place today. / At sunrise, does not the mass of darkness vanish in the cavern?"

Hearing that, O king, Lomaśa, his heart softened with compassion, / of great splendor, replied to that sage who was grieving for his son:

6.127.m:
"By my grace, let memory be born instantly in the youths; / and I shall declare that dharma by which their mutual curse will come to an end."

Vedanidhi said: / "O great sage, tell the dharma by which the youths may be freed. / This is no time for delay, since the fire of the curse is dreadful."

Lomaśa said: / "Together with me, let them perform the Māgha bath according to rule; / they will be freed from the curse at the end of Māgha—otherwise there can be no expiation.

A curse is the fruit of sin, O brāhmaṇa; the destruction of sin occurs for men / through the Māgha bath in a sacred ford—such is my settled view.

Sin committed in seven lifetimes, as well as current sin, / the Māgha bath burns up completely, especially at a sacred ford.

For whatever sin the lordly sages see no expiation, / even that sin is destroyed at holy sacred fords through Māgha.

At Mānasa, the Māgha [bath] creates knowledge; therefore it yields the fruit of liberation. / In the sacred fords on the slopes of the Himavat, it destroys all sin.

At Acchoda, it is declared by the speakers of the Veda to grant the world of Indra. / In the Badarī forest, the Māgha [bath] removes all sins and grants liberation.

At the Narmadā, the Māgha [bath] destroys sin, takes away sorrow, / grants the fruit of all desires, gives the world of Rudra, and removes sins.

6.127.m:
That of the Yamunā destroys blemishes and leads to the world of the sun; / that of the Sarasvatī annihilates evil and yields the fruit of the world of Brahmā.

At Viśālā, O best of the twice-born, the Māgha [bath] gives vast results; / it is a forest fire to the fuel of sin and removes actions that cause rebirth.

That of the Jāhnavī is proclaimed to lead to the world of Viṣṇu and to liberation. / At the Śarayū, Gaṇḍakī, Sindhu, Candrabhāgā, Kauśikī,

Tāpī, Godāvarī, Bhīmā, Payoṣṇī, Kṛṣṇaveṇikā, / Kāverī, Tuṅgabhadrā, and other rivers that flow into the sea,

a man bathing in Māgha quickly goes to the heavenly world, freed from stain. / At Naimiṣa, he attains union with Viṣṇu; at Puṣkara, the presence of Brahmā.

At Kurukṣetra through Māgha, one reaches the world of Indra; / at Devahrada, O brāhmaṇa, the Māgha [bath] yields the fruit of success in yoga.

At Prabhāsa when the sun is in Capricorn, from bathing one becomes an attendant of Rudra; / at Devakī, a man obtains a divine body through Māgha.

By the Māgha bath at the Gomatī, O brāhmaṇa, there is no rebirth. / At Hemakūṭa, Mahākāla, Oṃkāra, and Amareśvara,

At Nīlakaṇṭha and on Arbuda, because of Māgha one is honored in the realm of Rudra; / and at the confluence of all rivers, O brahmin, when the sun is in Capricorn,

by bathing, all desires of mortals are attained. / But Māgha [bath] at Prayāga is attained by the fortunate, O best among the twice-born, / since the dark and white waters there grant freedom from rebirth.

The gods dwelling in heaven constantly sing: ‘Indeed, will there be Māgha for us at Prayāga, / where, through bathing, mortals do not experience the pain of the womb and dwell in the presence of Viṣṇu?’

Even those men covered in abundant sins who bathe for three days here at the holy ford of Prayāga / do not go to the hells; becoming righteous, they roam delightfully like gods in the auspicious heaven.

Formerly, [Prayāga] was placed on a scale by the Creator along with holy fords, vows, gifts, penances, and sacrifices; / of the two, the [bath] of Prayāga in Māgha proved heavier, and for that reason it is superior.

The state that men attain through severe austerities accumulated over a long time—subsisting on wind, water, and dry leaves, drying up the body— / and through yogas, they attain that very state by bathing in Māgha.

And when the sun rises in Capricorn at the holy ford of Prayāga, at the confluence with the divine river, / does not a swarm of bees struck by the ears of elephants adorn the doorway of the house of those who bathe there?

6.127.m:
Why should that Prayāga not be resorted to, which grants through bathing a reward greater than the Rājasūya and horse sacrifices, / having destroyed all sins with ease?

Formerly, in the region of Avanti, there was a king named Vīrasena; / having gone to the bank of the Narmadā, he performed a Rājasūya,

and with sixteen horse sacrifices adorned with golden enclosures, / rich in sacrificial posts adorned with golden ornaments, he sacrificed according to the rules.

He gave heaps of grain like mountains to the twice-born; / generous, devoted to the deities, he gave cows and he gave gold.

There was a brahmin named Bhadraka, foolish and of low lineage, / an agriculturalist, of bad conduct, excluded from all duties.

Troubled by farming work and not cared for by his kin, / wandering here and there, he went away, tormented by hunger.

By providence joining a caravan, he arrived at Prayāga; / observing the Great Māghī, he bathed there for three days.

Having become sinless merely by bathing, that twice-born / departed from Prayāga back to the place from which he had come.

Once, both that king and the brahmin died at the same time; / their equal destination was seen by me in the presence of Śakra.

Their splendor, form, strength, women, celestial car, ornaments, / garland made of pārijāta flowers, dance, and music were all equal.

"Such glorification of the sacred site is observed; how can it be described? / Māgha at the confluence of the white and dark [rivers], O Brahmin, is considered equal to rājasūya sacrifices.

At the confluence of the white and dark waters extending for three hundred bows, / the Māgha [bath] yields freedom from rebirth, [whereas] the Rājasūya leads to rebirth again.

Even the wind of the month of Māgha touches the dark and white waters; / surely, [sin] cannot touch the unrighteous, for it destroys even great sins.

What is the use of speaking much here? Let it be heard with certainty, O twice-born: / Māgha at the holy ford destroys sins whose fruits have already arisen.

In this regard I will relate to you—listen with attentive mind— / an ancient legendary history called 'The Release of the Piśāca.'"

Let the young apsarases listen, and likewise let your son listen; / by my grace, those desiring release from the condition of a piśāca obtained remembrance.

Formerly, the brahmin Devadyuti, a Vaiṣṇava who had mastered the Vedas,

released piśācas, his mind overflowing with compassion.

Dilīpa said: / Where did he dwell? Whose son was he? What was his observance or recitation? / Or how did he become a Vaiṣṇava, and which piśācas were released?

6.127.m: and with mālatīs, mogarās, adorned with nutmeg trees; / with punnāgas and kiṃśukas, and sweet-basil and tulasī shrubs.
The hermitage was delightful with diverse kinds of trees, O king; / through the middle of the forest flowed the Sarasvatī with its holy waters.
There sarus cranes always cry out with indistinct, intoxicated, and melodious notes; / cuckoos make their sound, and bees hum.
The forest was full of clamor caused by parrots and mainas, O king; / various wild beasts roamed there in the best of forests.
It had perpetual fruit and flowers, was grey with pollen dust, / and the whole forest was covered all around with madhu trees.
Clasped on all sides by creepers bearing clusters produced from new shoots, / it was charming, like a lover embraced by his beloved women.
Afraid of his curse, the wind blew softly all around; / clouds did not rain down with hailstones, nor did the sun scorch.
that forest was free from affliction, continually resorted to by the perfected beings, / ever producing delight, like the Caitraratha forest.
In that [forest] lived the righteous Devadyuti, the best among the twice-born, / the son of the brahmin Sumitra, obtained by a boon from the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Hear the observance of him whose mind was always restrained: / in summer, he was constantly amid five fires, fixing his gaze upon the sun.
As long as the mass of clouds rained, he stayed in the open space under the sky in the rainy season; / when the wind blew, he was motionless and unendurable like the Himavat.
In winter he lived in the waters, in a pool of the Sarasvatī, O twice-born; / at the proper time, he touched the pure water three times [daily].
With faith, he constantly satisfied the ancestors, gods, and sages; / always dedicated to Vedic study, truthful in speech, with his senses subdued,
having rested on the ground when tired, he meditated, praying to Hari; / he offered the agnihotra with wild grains, and with faith honored guests.
He passed his time always in accordance with the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow; / he sought his livelihood through fallen leaves and fruits.
Undisturbed, steadfast in austerity, master of the Vedas and auxiliary disciplines, / his veins were prominent, and his body was mere bone.
In this manner, a thousand years passed for him in the forest; / then that mountain blazed with the heat of his austerity.
The beings could not endure the heat of that great-souled one; / he shone like fire, blazing through austerity, O twice-born.
Creatures in that forest lost their enmities; / deer and tigers, mice and cats played together without fear.
Hear also of another exceedingly rare observance of his: / he constantly worshipped Nārāyaṇa at the three times of day,
with a thousand blooming, fragrant flowers, / according to the rite of Vedic hymns, intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu.
For the pleasure of Viṣṇu, the brahmin performed all duties; / by the gift of Dadhīci's boon, he had become an excellent Vaiṣṇava.
Once, in the month of Vaiśākha on the eleventh day, the great sage, / having performed a lovely worship of Hari, uttered a wondrous hymn of praise.
Just then, mounting the bird, the God of gods, Hari himself, / came before him, exceedingly delighted by that hymn.
Seeing him mounted on Garuḍa, visible before his eyes, with the luster of a cloud, / four-armed, broad-eyed, adorned with all ornaments,
the brahmin's hair stood on end, his eyes filled with tears of joy; / with a mind fulfilled, he then bowed his head to the earth.
Through that joy he could not be contained even within the egg of Brahmā; / he did not remember his own body, and became as though absorbed in Brahman.
Then the Vaiṣṇava sage was addressed with affection by Hari: / 'O Devadyuti, I know that you are my devotee, taking refuge in me.
You have renounced all actions, your being is in me, and your mind is ever on me; / choose a boon, for I am pleased by this hymn of praise, O sinless one.'
Hearing these words of Hari, that ascetic replied: / "O god of gods, lotus-eyed one, who have assumed a form through your own māyā!
O God, from your sight no other boon is ever so difficult to obtain; / all the gods beginning with Brahmā, yogins like Sanaka and others,
and perfected ones like Kapila desire to see you face to face. / The snares of "I" and "mine", delusion and greed, both auspicious and inauspicious,
together with their causes, are burned away when you, the higher and the lower, are seen. / The fruit of my birth, my action, and my intellect has manifested,
since you have been seen, O Lord of the world! What more can I ask than this? / Truly, not for the sake of a boon, O Lord of the gods, do I contemplate
your lotus feet in my heart always with devotion, my inner self fixed on you. / I ask for this boon alone: may my devotion to you be unshakeable!
Let it be so, O Lord of Kamalā! I ask for no other boon.' / Hearing his words, Hari, with a pleased countenance
and a gracious mind, replied: 'So be it, O best of the twice-born! / There shall be no other obstacle whatsoever to your austerity.
And whatever men shall recite this hymn composed by you, / their devotion toward me shall be steadfast.
And whatever duty they undertake shall be completely fulfilled with all its parts; / and their supreme devotion to spiritual knowledge shall remain unwavering.'
Having spoken thus, Janārdana, the god of gods, disappeared there. / From that time on, Devadyuti became wholly devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Dilīpa said: / 'O great sage, I am favored; I have been purified by this story, / as if by the Gaṅgā today through this connection with Viṣṇu.
Tell me what that hymn of praise was, by which Mādhava was pleased / with that sinless brahmin; great is my curiosity.
By your grace, O brahmin, I consider my wish to be attained; / for whose greatness does association with the great not serve?
Graciously recite the supreme hymn of Viṣṇu, / pleased with which the Blessed Lord granted him his vision.'
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'I shall tell you that secret, the supreme hymn that was recited, / which was first received by the beautiful-winged Garuḍa and passed from Garuḍa to me.
It holds the essence of the inner Self; it produces great fortune and is auspicious; / it removes all sins, O king, and grants the supreme knowledge of one's own Self.
Om, salutations to Vāsudeva, salutations to the All, the wielder of the discus, / dear to devotees, to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the world, wielder of the bow Śārṅga!
When the praiser, the praised, and the praise—the whole world—consists of Viṣṇu, / then by whom is he praised? Yet devotion brings delight to mortals.
Of which God the breath is the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs and sūtras— / what praise could delight him? Yet through devotion I have become talkative.
All the three worlds, with the moving and unmoving, turn like a wheel; / therefore you are praised, O God, whose hand bears the discus, an excellent weapon.
Whom the Veda does not describe directly, nor does speech know, nor the mind; / how can someone like me praise him, or how could one become devoted?

Beginning with Brahmā, you are Brahman and Viṣṇu; you alone are the refuge of all; / you are the creator, O Brahman, the primary cause, and pure Brahman itself.

"What body is this of yours, O Lord, which, having pierced, touches the embodied soul, / yet is not touched by the faults of the body? Salutation to that yogin!
In the divine state one is awake, not sleeping in one's own self; / that intellect which is an abundance of bliss—that are you, O Viṣṇu, beyond doubt.
The cosmic intellect and the rest are the great realities, as well as the modified qualities; / you alone, O Lord, are all that; diversity is a conception of the foolish.
Through three conceptions, with the forms of Keśa, Keśava, and others, / you alone are conceived, O Brahman, like a man through sons and relatives.
Faultless, without qualities, the one conscious embodiment of the entire world, / the reality that shines to wise seers—I bow to that stainless Viṣṇu.
Through knowledge of whom, those free from craving and friends of the world / perform even the actions prescribed by scripture—to that pure Brahman I bow.
When other things are dissolved, yogins, through his awakening, / worship that which is mere existence in all beings—to that Hari, who is true being, I bow.
Knowing whom alone, excellent twice-born ones sing, "I am Brahman," / seeing no deity equal to you—I bow to Mādhava.
Who destroys the manifold delusions caused by māyā, and mortals' sense of "I" and "mine", / as well as streams of sins—salutations to that embodiment of consciousness!
Remembering whose name at the time of departure or not, / mortals' heaps of sins are instantly destroyed—salutations to that embodiment of consciousness!
While the worlds burn continually with the blazing flames of the fire of delusion, / one who enters the shade of his lotus feet is not burned.
By the mere remembrance of whom there is no delusion, no misfortune, / no diseases, and no sorrows—to that Infinite One I bow.
Arising from their intellects, they desire no offspring; / those people, walking solitary in awakening, see the world as the Self alone.
If the meaning of word and the meaning of consciousness are the highest name of Viṣṇu, / by that truth may worldly existence not touch me, O Mādhava!
If Nārāyaṇa pervades the universe, as accepted by the Vedas and other scriptures, / by that truth let my devotion to Viṣṇu be free of obstacles!
He who is without a seed, yet the seed; who is contemplated as the seed within the seed; / may that Viṣṇu cut down the seed of my rebirth with the sword of white knowledge.
He who, having three bodies like an actor in creation, maintenance, and dissolution, / manifests through the qualities in his actions—may that Hari be pleased with me!
He who descended ten times solely to protect dharma, / requested by all the gods—may that Hari be pleased with me!
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, in the temple of the heart of living beings, / the one stainless God who dwells—may that Hari be pleased with me!
In the beginning that Being made a wish: 'May I be one and also many'; / the creator who entered the deities—may that Hari be pleased with me!

You move in the sky of the heart, are like the sky, originate the sky, are beyond the sky, act through the sky, move in space; / you are the sky, you are Brahmā, you consume the sky and the rest, and at the end your form is space, O consumer of sacrifices.
By whose light, by whose delight, by whose power of illusion the world is produced; / yet inertness, sorrow, and unreality are also You, consisting of them.
Created by You the universe rejoices, and abandoned by You it becomes impure; / though connected with it, You are unattached, and by that You undergo no modification.
The Cārvākas worship that consciousness which arises from the combination of the elements; / the Buddhists say through reasoning that You are consciousness that is momentary and perishable.
The Jinas consider You to have the measure of the body; / the followers of Sāṅkhya meditate upon You alone as the spirit beyond nature.
Free from birth and the like, that which in the beginning has the nature of bliss— / it is You alone whom the Upaniṣads contemplate mutually as Brahman.
The elements beginning with space, the body, mind, intellect, and the senses, / knowledge and ignorance—all are You alone here; there is nothing whatever other than You.
You are the creator of all beings; You alone are my refuge. / You are the fire, You are the oblation, Śakra, the hotṛ priest, the mantra, the rite, and the fruit.
You are existence and nonexistence, O Vaikuṇṭha; I have gone to You for refuge. / You are the giver of the fruit of actions, and the fruit of the rites of the initiated.
You are the cause of all beings; You alone are my refuge. / As the mind of young women delights in a young man, and as that of young men delights in a young woman,
so may my love delight in You. / Even if a man is sinful and ill-behaved, when he bows down to You, O Hari,
the servants of Yama do not look at him, just as owls do not look at the sun. / The threefold suffering and the mass of sins torment a person only so long,
O Lord, as he does not remember Your lotus-feet with devotion.

Whom the qualities, caste, and physical characteristics do not touch, whom the movements of all the sense organs do not touch, / and whom the sages, free from attachment and delusion, touch—to that Lord Hari I bow down.

Dissolving the gross into the organ, the organ into the first cause, and that cause into that which is devoid of organ and cause— / having thus dissolved them, the sages enter there; praise be to that Hari who is served by sages.

Whom meditating upon, having subdued by whirling movement the fortune of liberation and bliss possessed of charming qualities of sovereignty, / embracing her, they lie down, enjoying only the bliss of the Self; praise be to that Hari who is served by sages.

In whose nature, free from transformations of existence such as birth, this group of six waves is dispersed, / whom the faults such as passion do not constantly torment—to that pure Vāsudeva dwelling in the heart I bow."

Absorbed in meditating on whom, the mind abandons ignorance; fallen into the fire of whose meditation, the world meets destruction; / whose flashing knowledge destroys the enemy that is doubt—to that You, Hari, a mass of pure consciousness, I bow down.
All beings moving and unmoving are under Hari's control; / as this is true, by that truth let Hari stand before me.
As Nārāyaṇa is the whole world, stationary and moving, / by that truth let Keśava show his form to me.
As I have devotion to Hari, and if there is highest devotion to the guru / in me, by that truth let Keśava show himself.
Thus, through his true oaths, considering his devotion, / Puruṣottama, pleased, revealed himself.
Then, having given him a boon and fulfilled his desire, / the beloved of Kamalā, satisfied by the brahmin with praise, departed.
That twice-born too, his purpose accomplished, devoted to Vāsudeva, / chanting the hymn along with his disciples, stayed in that penance grove.
Whatever human proclaims this hymn of praise, or even hears it, / obtains the vast fruit of the horse sacrifice.
A brāhmaṇa always attains the awakening of knowledge of the Self; / his mind does not incline toward sin, nor does he see inauspiciousness.
Soundness of intellect, soundness of mind, and soundness of the senses / accrue to all people from reciting this hymn of praise.
A person who, having reflected upon its meaning, recites it attentively with faith, / shaking off sins in this world, attains the realm of Viṣṇu.
He obtains his desired wishes: sons, grandsons, and cattle; / reciting it constantly, he obtains long life, strength, and vigor.
The fruit that is obtained from a thousand vessels of sesame or a thousand cows, / that fruit a person obtains who proclaims this praise.
Whatever of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation he constantly desires, / that a human being attains before long by means of this hymn of praise.
In conduct, humility, dharma, knowledge, austerity, and good guidance, / the intellect of people who listen attentively to this praise is ever established.
Whether endowed with great sins or endowed with minor sins, / by a single recitation of the hymn of praise, one instantly becomes pure in soul.
It promotes wisdom, prosperity, renown, fame, knowledge, and dharma; / it calms malevolent planets and destroys all inauspiciousness.
Removing all diseases, wholesome, destroying all calamities, / a means of crossing through misfortune, this hymn of praise should be recited by the twice-born.
During affliction from asterisms and planets, in fears from kings or thieves, / and in attacks by fire or thieves, one should immediately proclaim this.
There is no fear of lions or tigers, nor fear of sorcery, / nor from spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and rākṣasas,
nor from Pūtanās, Jṛmbhakas, or obstacles at any time; / there is nowhere any fear for people when this hymn of praise is proclaimed.
He who, having performed worship of Vāsudeva, utters this hymn of praise, / is not stained by sins, just as a lotus leaf is not stained by water.
That destination which is not attained by baths in holy places such as the Gaṅgā, / that destination one attains reciting this auspicious praise.
He who recites it once, twice, or thrice a day, / always, at all times, enjoys imperishable happiness.
The fruit that comes from reciting all four Vedas three times over, / that fruit a person obtains by reading this hymn of praise once.
He obtains inexhaustible wealth, becomes dear to women, / and receives worship in this world, remembering Hari with faith.
Always endowed with prosperity, he never comes to misfortune; / he is not carried away by speech, who daily proclaims this praise.
Misfortune, Kā Karṇī, bad dreams, and evil thoughts / are instantly destroyed for the devotees who listen attentively to this praise.
Having risen at dawn, he who reads it, being pure and devoted to Viṣṇu, / obtains imperishable happiness in this world and the next.
Composed by Devadyuti, pleasing to Viṣṇu, auspicious, / producing Viṣṇu's favor, causing the vision of Viṣṇu,
this supremely purifying hymn of praise named Yogasāra— / he who recites it constantly with devotion goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.

"Thus has been told to you the secret hymn that destroys sins. / Henceforth I shall describe the liberation of the piśāca."

Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, / in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the glorification of Māgha, in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa, / ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, named "The Recitation of the Yogasāra Hymn."
